planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Roma is sterile and produces no seed, so all propagation is by division of the clump.

directions: Roma bears rose-red pincushion flowers ringed by a shallow starry cup of light silver-pink bracts, a subtler and more silvery pink than many masterwort cultivars. Because it is sterile it channels its energy into a remarkably long bloom season, flowering from late spring into midsummer and often again in early autumn if spent stems are cut back after the first flush. Plant in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, where cool summers keep the clump vigorous and prevent premature summer dormancy. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain flowering vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in sun to partial shade; Buckland is a taller, bushier selection believed to be a hybrid of A. major and A. maxima.

directions: Buckland is a taller, upright masterwort named by plantsman Alan Bloom, carrying finely etched, dusty silvery-pink florets each cradled in a papery, silvery-green ruff of bracts. It is among the longest-flowering of all the masterworts, blooming steadily from early summer well into autumn, especially if faded stems are trimmed back to encourage repeat flushes. Grow in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade, though it tolerates more sun than most masterworts where soil stays consistently moist. The long-lasting flowers hold up well as cut stems for arrangements. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Venice is among the darkest-flowered masterwort cultivars and holds its rich color best in cool conditions.

directions: Venice produces some of the darkest flowers found in the genus, with a dense, dark ruby-red to wine-colored pincushion of florets set within a matching ring of deep reddish-purple bracts. The intense coloring makes it a striking accent against the paler pinks and whites of most masterworts, and the wiry stems are sturdy enough to need no staking. Plant in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, where the color develops most fully and blooms continue from early summer into autumn with deadheading. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Star of Billion Masterwort (White Cut-Flower Masterwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Star of Billion grows slightly taller than most masterwort cultivars and was bred for cut-flower production.

directions: Star of Billion carries large clusters of small flowers crowded atop branching stems, each framed by strap-shaped white bracts tipped in green; the flowers open pale green, blush soft pink as they mature, and finish paper-white, giving the umbels a shifting, multi-toned effect over the long June-to-September bloom season. Despite its taller, airier habit it is sturdier than it looks and rarely needs staking. Grow in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, and use the long-lasting stems for cutting, since they hold up well in both fresh and dried arrangements. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; variegation is strongest on fresh spring growth and fades toward green as the season progresses, so this cultivar is prized primarily for its spring display.

directions: Sunningdale Variegated is grown chiefly for its spectacular spring foliage: the hand-shaped, palmately lobed leaves emerge generously margined and streaked in gold and creamy yellow, a display considered by many gardeners the finest variegated foliage of the season. The variegation is strongest on young growth in part sun and gradually fades to green by summer, when the plant sends up wiry stems topped with the typical creamy-white, pink-tinged pincushion flowers. Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and remove any all-green reverted shoots promptly to keep the variegation from being lost from the clump. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost in well-drained soil; Red Knight blooms the first year from an early start and self-sows modestly once established.

directions: Red Knight bears bright, saturated crimson-red pincushion flowers on long, wiry, branching stems above a low mound of lobed basal foliage, a bolder and more vivid red than the straight species' typical wine-purple tones. It flowers continuously from early summer through the first hard frost if deadheaded regularly, and the airy, see-through habit makes it an excellent weaver through borders and gravel gardens. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps tolerate considerable summer drought. The nectar-rich flowers draw bees and butterflies in steady numbers throughout the bloom season.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring in average to moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike F. ulmaria this Japanese species tolerates soil that is merely evenly moist rather than boggy.

directions: Japanese meadowsweet is a native of moist Japanese meadows and streambanks, producing purple-tinged stems topped with branched, astilbe-like sprays of deep crimson-pink flowers — the richest pink of any Filipendula — from early to midsummer above broad, serrated, palmately lobed leaves. It is more tolerant of average garden moisture than the boggy F. ulmaria, though it still performs best where soil never dries out fully. Grow in humus-rich soil in partial shade, or full sun where moisture is reliable, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor. The nectar-rich flowers are attractive to butterflies and other pollinators.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Multiplex Double Dropwort (Flore Pleno Double-Flowered Dropwort)

planting.note: Divide established plants in spring or fall into well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; like the species, Multiplex prefers dry, calcareous conditions and performs poorly in wet soil.

directions: Multiplex (also sold as Flore Pleno) is the ornamental double-flowered form of dropwort, bearing coral-bronze buds that open into small, tightly packed, creamy-white double 'roses' held in airy sprays on wiry bronze-tinged stems above the finely cut, fern-like foliage. It is noticeably showier and longer-lasting in bloom than the single-flowered species, since the doubled flowers do not set seed as readily and remain attractive for weeks. Plant in lean, well-drained, chalky or gravelly soil in full sun; like all dropworts it is intolerant of wet or heavy soil and should be kept out of moist border conditions that suit its meadowsweet relatives. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into moderately fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Tanna stays far more compact than the straight species and is well suited to smaller borders.

directions: Tanna is a compact, Award of Garden Merit-winning selection of great burnet, forming a neat mound of finely divided, crimped blue-green foliage well below the height of the species, topped by numerous wiry stems carrying deep red bottlebrush blooms from late summer into fall. Its low, dense habit makes it far more manageable than typical great burnet in small borders and mixed containers, while still providing the same late-season color and texture prized in naturalistic plantings. Grow in moderately fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and divide expanding clumps every few years in spring to maintain a tidy habit. The late blooms are valuable for pollinators heading into autumn.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this Japanese species is virtually pest and disease free and rabbit resistant once established.

directions: Japanese bottlebrush burnet is one of the most ornamental members of the genus, producing arching, wiry stems tipped with fluffy, nodding, soft pink bottlebrush spikes that sway gracefully in the breeze over a long summer bloom period. The grey-green, pinnately divided foliage forms a handsome low mound even when not in flower, distinguishing it from the narrower, more upright habit of S. tenuifolia. Grow in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it where afternoon shade is available in hot climates to prolong the bloom display. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to refresh vigor; established plants are largely trouble-free and unappealing to rabbits.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist to wet, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; in the wild this species grows in coastal bogs and marshes from Alaska to Washington's Olympic Peninsula.

directions: Menzies' burnet is a Pacific Northwest native forming a low, clump-forming mound of finely divided, blue-green foliage, with tight, intense maroon-purple bottlebrush flower heads carried on slender stems from early to late summer. In its native coastal bogs and marshes it grows in consistently saturated, cool soil, and it performs best in cultivation with the same steady moisture in a rain garden, bog garden, or pond margin. Grow in moderately fertile, moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; it is intolerant of prolonged drought. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and share this uncommon native burnet with other gardeners.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)
